newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen has less upside than other dollar pairs.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen has less upside than other dollar pairs.

text.p: This weekend's Group-of-Seven (G7) statement does nothing to alter the dollar's bullish fundamentals, but dollar/yen has less upside potential than other dollar currency pairs, analysts said on Monday.

With short-term Japanese interest rates less than 0.5 percent compared with the U.S. at over 5.0 percent, and the Japanese economy in a sorry state compared with the U.S., it would seem that dollar/yen has much further to go.
But there is no escaping the fact that dollar/yen has risen a massive 55 percent in less than two years.
"Anything over 125 yen and it's starting to look too high, a bit like sterling/dollar does when it gets above $1.65," said Chris Tinker, Chief Treasury Economist at Standard Chartered.
"It can certainly go higher, above 125, but at that point the market is going to start to believe it is not sustainable."

Of the G7 countries Japan is clearly the most worried about the strong dollar -- at G7 they said the yen's decline was "rather rapid" -- but within the rest of G7 there is a degree of self interest in not seeing the yen weaken further.

Japanese markets and the banking sector are currently looking extremely shaky and a further yen decline would not help. It is the follow-on impact of possible financial turmoil in Japan that worries G7, analysts said.
The situation in dollar/yen at 120 on the way up is reminiscent of dollar/yen at 90 when it was coming down in 1995.
The authorities were then talking it higher, even the fundamentals were not arguing for a further fall, but the momentum was so strong it continued to slide.
In seven weeks dollar/yen fell around 18 percent from 97.2 to the 79.70 low.

"I think they are very keen to avoid a similar overshoot this time on the upside because G7 are worried about the impact on Japan and a ripple effect globally on financial markets," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Banque Paribas.
In addition to its already impressive rise dollar/yen will also be restrained by the fact that the Bank of Japan has over $200 billion of reserves to sell to keep it down.

Japan's reserves built up during the dollar's slide in early 1995 when the Japanese authorities were desperately trying to push dollar/yen higher to save an exporting industry which was being hammered by the yen's uncompetitive firmness.
Any dealer who is aggressively long of dollar/yen above 125 could find that the Bank of Japan is suddenly his counter-party.
"How far it goes depends a lot on whether capital continues to flow out of Japan," said Tobert Hayward, economic adviser at BankAmerica.
When the new Japanese fiscal year begins on April 1 funds could start to move back into Japan if the economy looks more positive. But analysts said it was unclear whether that would happen.

"I think we will see a more cautious move higher and as the fiscal year commences we could see a moderation of captial outflow which at the end of the day will be more important than comments from Japanese officials," Hayward said.
